opus-5.5.text:
Well, it came out of a frustration, really. In the 1990s, when I was working on image segmentation, the field had a problem: everybody would propose an algorithm, run it on a handful of images, show you the pictures, and say, "Look, this looks good." And how do you argue with that? You'd look at someone else's results and they'd also look sort of good. There was no way to make progress in a cumulative, scientific way. It was more like an art exhibition than a science.

So the question I kept asking myself was: what is the ground truth for segmentation? It's not obvious, because segmentation is somewhat subjective. If you ask different people to divide an image into regions, they won't give you exactly the same answer. One person will outline the whole person, another will separate the face from the shirt. For a while that ambiguity was used as an excuse: segmentation is ill-defined, so we can't measure it.

What we found, when my students and I built the Berkeley Segmentation Dataset, was that human segmentations are actually remarkably consistent once you account for refinement. People differ in granularity, but they're not contradicting each other; one segmentation is mostly a refinement of the other. That was a scientific finding in itself. It told us there's a real, measurable signal in human perception, and that gave us a basis for defining benchmarks and metrics, like precision-recall on boundaries, that you could actually trust.

And once you have that, things change. You can compare algorithms honestly. You can see whether learning from data helps, and it did: we showed that learning to combine brightness, color, and texture cues from human-labeled data beat hand-designed edge detectors. So the dataset wasn't just an evaluation tool; it became the training signal.

I've always thought of it in terms of psychophysics. Human annotation, done carefully, is a kind of measurement of human perception. It's the closest thing we have to an operational definition of what the visual system is supposed to compute. If you take that seriously, then datasets and benchmarks aren't bookkeeping. They're how you turn vision from a collection of clever demos into an empirical science.

Of course, I'd add a caution. Benchmarks can also become a trap. People start optimizing the number rather than understanding the problem. So I see them as necessary but not sufficient. They keep us honest, but they shouldn't define the entire research agenda.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that it came out of a sense of frustration with how the field was operating in the early days. When I started in computer vision in the 1980s, the way research was done was that somebody would have an idea, write an algorithm, run it on a handful of images, maybe five or ten, and publish the results. There was no way to compare one approach to another. Everybody had their own favorite images, their own favorite examples, and a lot of the arguments were essentially arguments of taste.

Now, I had come out of a tradition that took science seriously. I was influenced by people like David Marr, who thought about vision as a computational problem, and I always felt that if we were going to call this a science, we needed something that looked like empirical validation. In physics you have experiments and you have a ground truth. In vision, the question was, what is the ground truth? And the answer I eventually arrived at was that the ground truth, at least for a lot of perceptual tasks, is what humans perceive. Vision is in the end about reproducing capabilities that humans have, so human judgments are a very reasonable standard to measure against.

The concrete turning point for me was the work we did at Berkeley around 2000 on image segmentation. Segmentation at that point was a mess. Everybody had their own algorithm, and there was no agreed way to say that one was better than another. So we did something quite simple in retrospect: we collected a few hundred natural images, and we had human subjects draw the boundaries of the objects and regions they saw. That became the Berkeley Segmentation Dataset. And once you had that, you could actually ask, how close does an algorithm get to what people do? You could plot precision-recall curves, you could make quantitative progress, and the arguments shifted from matters of opinion to matters of evidence.

I should say there was some skepticism about this. People worried that humans disagree with each other, and of course they do. But what we found was that the disagreement was structured. Different people would segment at different levels of granularity, but they were rarely inconsistent with each other. One person's segmentation was typically a refinement of another's. So the human data was noisy, but it was not arbitrary, and that gave us confidence it could serve as a foundation.

The other thing that happened was that once you have a benchmark, you get an engine of progress. It creates a community. Students can enter the field, try an idea, and know within a week whether it works. And that model then spread, through PASCAL VOC, through ImageNet, to the whole of the field. I think the deep learning revolution in vision is almost unimaginable without that infrastructure, because it's what allowed people to see that these methods were actually working, and working dramatically better than the alternatives.

So I would put it this way. Benchmarks and human annotations were not the goal of the science. The goal was understanding vision. But they were the instrument that let us do science at all, rather than something closer to philosophy.

astra-6.text:
Well, computer vision needs a way to connect its theories to observations. You can propose an algorithm and show a few attractive examples, but that doesn’t tell you how well it works in general. You need a collection of images, a clearly defined task, and some independent basis for judging the answers.

Human annotations provide that basis for many perceptual tasks. If we want a computer to find boundaries or recognize objects, it makes sense to ask what people see. But you have to be careful: an annotation is a measurement of human judgment, and people may disagree. In segmentation, for example, one person might mark an object as a whole, while another marks its parts. That variation is something to understand, rather than simply discard.

A benchmark then gives researchers a shared experiment. Different approaches can be tested on the same problem, and we can learn which ideas actually improve performance. The important thing is to keep asking whether the measurement captures the visual ability we care about. A benchmark is useful because it makes a scientific question testable; the score itself is not the scientific question.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it came from the realization that if we wanted to make progress in vision, we needed to be able to measure it. It is very easy to show a few pictures on which your algorithm does something interesting. But how do you know whether the underlying idea is actually better? You need a common set of images, a clearly defined task, and a way of comparing the output with what people perceive.

Segmentation made this particularly clear. Ask a person to divide an image into regions, and there isn’t necessarily one uniquely correct answer. One person might mark an entire person; another might also mark the face, the arms, and the clothing. So human annotations shouldn’t simply be treated as an infallible answer key. Having several people annotate the same image lets you understand the variability in the task and gives you a meaningful standard against which to evaluate an algorithm.

That was the spirit behind the Berkeley segmentation dataset and benchmark: make the data and the evaluation available so that different ideas could be tested on common ground. Then the field can accumulate knowledge. A benchmark is valuable because it makes a claim testable, but you must always remember that the scientific objective is understanding vision, not merely improving a number.
